chunks: When to use plugged vias. The question: When would I want plugged vias?
A plugged via has its hole blocked with soldermask ink (the board's thin colored coating) or epoxy resin, so nothing can pass through.
It is not sanded flat and plated over, so its surface is not a good solder pad.
You use plugged vias to stop solder being sucked in or bridging between pads, to make a board airtight for vacuum test fixtures, and to avoid trapping chemicals.
For a via in a solder pad you need a filled and capped via instead.
Think of a pipe. Tenting is like stretching plastic wrap over the pipe's end. The pipe is still hollow, and the wrap can pop. Plugging is like pushing a cork into the pipe.
Nothing can pass and nothing can pop through, but the cork may stick up. Filling and capping is sanding the cork flush and covering it with a flat lid.
Only that is smooth enough to stand on.
A sketch of the IPC-4761 progression (simplified, one side shown). Types I and II leave the barrel hollow. Types III and IV block it.
Types V to VII fill it completely, and only VII ends with a copper cap that makes a flat solderable pad. Real cross-sections vary by fab.
Tenting: covering a via's opening with a film of soldermask, leaving the hole hollow. Plugging: blocking the hole with ink or epoxy.
Filled and capped: filled, sanded flat and plated over with copper. Solder wicking: solder being pulled into an open via.
Vacuum test fixture: a test jig that sucks the board against probes, so the board must be airtight. IPC-4761: the standard that names the types of via protection.
A vacuum fixture pulls on the board, so every open hole is a leak. A 0. 3 mm via has an opening of about 0. 07 mm².
A board with 2,000 open vias then has a total leak area of about 141 mm². That is small next to the board, but it can still defeat the vacuum, depending on the pump and gasket.
Plugging the vias seals them. That is the whole idea: a plug blocks the hole but does not make a flat pad.
"A plugged via has its barrel blocked with soldermask or epoxy, but it isn't ground flat or plated over like a filled via.
I use plugging to stop solder wicking and shorts near pads or on wave-soldered sides, to make the board airtight for vacuum test fixtures, and to avoid trapped chemicals or ingress.
It's not enough for via-in-pad, which needs filled and capped, and it costs more than tenting, so I use it only where tenting isn't robust enough."
